pages.text: On a clear night with no Moon, far from town lights, a pale band of light stretches across the sky. People in many cultures have told stories about it. The ancient Greeks thought it looked like spilt milk, and that is where the name Milky Way comes from. In 1610, Galileo pointed a telescope at the band and saw that it is made of countless faint stars. We now know that it is our own galaxy, seen from the inside. A galaxy is an enormous collection of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter, all held together by gravity.

pages.alt: The band of the Milky Way arching over a dark Ghanaian savanna landscape with a baobab tree in silhouette.

pages.text: The Milky Way holds at least 100 billion stars, and perhaps as many as 400 billion. It is shaped like a flat disc with a bulge in the middle, about 100,000 light-years across. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Curved arms of stars wind out from the centre, so astronomers call it a spiral galaxy. The Sun sits in one of the smaller arms, about 26,000 light-years from the centre. The whole Solar System is orbiting the centre of the galaxy at about 800,000 kilometres an hour. Even at that speed, one trip round takes about 230 million years.

pages.text: At the centre of the Milky Way sits a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A* (say “Sagittarius A-star”). A black hole is not an empty hole. It is a huge amount of matter squeezed into a tiny space. Its gravity is so strong that nothing that comes too close can escape, not even light. Sagittarius A* has about four million times the mass of the Sun. Astronomers showed it was there by tracking stars that whip around it, work that won a Nobel Prize in 2020. In 2022, a worldwide network of radio telescopes produced the first picture of the glowing gas around it. Earth is in no danger. We are 26,000 light-years away.

pages.text: Here is a puzzle. Stars near the edge of a galaxy orbit much faster than they should. The gravity of all the stars and gas we can see is too weak to hold them in. Something else must be adding gravity. Astronomers call it dark matter. It gives out no light, so no telescope can see it directly. We know it only by its pull. Measurements suggest that about 85 per cent of all the matter in the universe is dark matter. Nobody yet knows what it is made of. It is one of the biggest unsolved questions in science.

pages.text: The Milky Way is one galaxy among a vast number, and they do not all look alike. Astronomers sort them into four main shapes. Spiral galaxies, like ours, are flat discs with curved arms. Elliptical galaxies are smooth and rounded, like a ball or an egg, with no arms. Lenticular galaxies are in between: a disc with a central bulge, shaped like a lens, but without clear arms. Irregular galaxies have no regular shape at all. Many of them were pulled out of shape by the gravity of a larger neighbour.

pages.text: The Milky Way belongs to a cluster of galaxies called the Local Group. It has three large spiral galaxies, the Milky Way, Andromeda, and Triangulum, and dozens of small ones. The whole group is about 10 million light-years across. Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away. On a very dark night you can see it without a telescope, as a faint smudge. It is the most distant thing the human eye can see. Andromeda is moving towards us. Astronomers used to predict a certain collision in about 4.5 billion years. A 2025 study found the chance is only about 50 per cent in the next 10 billion years.

activities.question: Which statement best describes the Milky Way?
options: A spiral galaxy containing at least 100 billion stars, including the Sun
A planet with a ring of dust
A cloud high in Earth’s atmosphere

activities.question: Why can light not escape from a black hole?
options: The black hole is completely empty
It is too cold for light to exist

activities.question: How do astronomers know that dark matter exists?
options: They have photographed it through large telescopes
Its gravity affects how fast stars orbit in galaxies

activities.question: Apply it: A telescope picture shows a smooth, rounded ball of stars with no disc and no arms. What type of galaxy is it?

items: One spiral arm of the Milky Way
